en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Worldly Wisdom: Chapter 1. The Section on the Wise.
I shall proclaim the worldly ethics,
extracted from various treatises,
in a concise summary in the Magadhi language.
Having paid homage to the Three Jewels:
In this world, the essence of a person consists of mother, father, teacher, and friend.
Therefore, a person should indeed understand the method;
one who possesses knowledge becomes great and is also well-learned.
How can there be craft for the lazy?
Whence can there be wealth for one who is not skilled in craft? Whence can there be a friend for one who has no wealth?
Whence can there be happiness for one who has no friend?
For one who lacks happiness, whence can there be merit?
For one who lacks merit, whence can there be excellence?
There is no wealth equal to crafts.
Thieves do not value craft;
in this world, craft is a friend,
and it brings happiness in the world beyond.
One should not despise even a small amount;
one should deposit what has been heard in the mind,
like a drop of water on an anthill.
Cirena one attains fulfillment.
One should not despise even a small thing,
whether it be knowledge or a craft.
Even a single pure [verse] is worth a lifetime's effort;
it is not like a ruby on every mountain.
Not in every elephant is there musk;
not in every forest is there sandalwood;
not in every place is there a wise man.
Wherever there is one who is wise, endowed with learning,
and possesses what he has heard—
by great effort, one should go to that place.
One who desires to hear must go,
as one who desires to learn a craft, one who desires wealth,
or one who desires to climb a mountain.
Attachment, desire, and anger—
these are the five attachments.
Tradition, convention, and number.
The yogas are the specialists;
the gandhabbas are the courtesans,
as well as the archers, the Vedas, and the Pūraṇas.
Medicine and history,
light and illusion,
desire; banner, mantra, and sounds.
These are the eighteen branches of the arts.
When unasked, I am wise;
when asked, I am like a drum or the rain-cloud.
Whether questioned or unasked,
a fool always speaks much;
and whatever craft is found in books, [he does not master it].
That wealth which lies in the hands of others when a need arises—
neither is that a craft, nor is that wealth.
The measure of water is the stalk of a white lotus;
the measure of a family is discipline;
the measure of eloquence is speech that has been well-spoken.
Just as a tiny speck of grass withers upon the earth,
so too the man of little learning, though he has heard but little, considers himself to have heard much.
Not seeing the water of the Indus,
like a frog in a well regarding the water in a well,
he first lost his craft.
In the second case, one loses wealth;
in the third, one loses the Dhamma;
what will the fourth case do?
The unskilled son is indolent, while the skilled one is a bearer of burdens;
the skilled one is honored in the world.
Day after day, the son becomes proficient;
the mother is the enemy and the father is the foe—
by whom was this child not taught?
They do not shine in the midst of an assembly,
like a crane in the midst of swans;
who could sharpen a thorn on a mountain?
Who is the collyrium for the eyes of deer?
Who is the fragrant path by the pond?
Who, appearing in the form of a son of noble family, wanders about?
The state of being oneself.
Not even betel with spices is a delight to one who is destitute, even if it be adorned.
Alaṅkāra is the ornament, grammar is the non-craft; obedience and being endowed with what has been heard—
these are the requisites for learning.
Through learning, wisdom increases;
through wisdom, one understands the meaning;
the understood meaning brings happiness.
Food, sexual intercourse,
and sleep are found even among oxen;
but knowledge is the distinguishing quality of a human being.
That inferior person would be like a cow.
There is no friend equal to knowledge,
nor is there an enemy equal to disease.
There is no love equal to that for oneself,
and no power equal to that of karma.
A swan is not among crows;
A lion does not shine among sheep;
a horse does not shine among donkeys,
nor does a wise man shine among fools.
Even if a fool attends upon a wise person for as long as he lives,
he does not understand the Dhamma.
Just as one takes up the flavor of the soup with a ladle,
if a wise person attends upon a learned one for even a moment;
One understands the Dhamma quickly,
just as the tongue perceives the taste of soup;
one should not go about without the Teacher.
A hero on the battlefield,
a wise man, a hunter, a merchant,
and likewise one traveling to a foreign land.
Loss of wealth, mental anguish,
misconduct within the home,
deception, and contempt.
A wise person should not display himself;
rather, one should speak words that are appropriate to the occasion, natural, and pleasing.
He who knows anger according to its own nature is wise;
he who tastes the flavor of one who has no wealth—
Men who lack strength are ruined;
the speech of one lacking wisdom is like that of a madman.
Leading one to what is unbeneficial,
speaking much without being asked,
and proclaiming one's own virtues—
There are three inferior characteristics:
one who is of little form but much talkative,
and one who is of little wisdom yet boastful.
A jar with little water is easily shaken;
a cow with little milk is easily agitated;
even a frog is a lion when provoked.
Even those who are not wise become wise by asking questions again and again, as dear to them as a crow’s eye.
A frog may be like a snake,
a lion like a pig,
and a leopard like a cat.
All the wise are alike in their craft:
a king has no satiety with wealth,
nor does a learned man with well-spoken words.
The eye is never sated by beautiful sights;
the ocean is not filled even by the waters of the sea.
[So it is with] those endowed with beauty and youth.
Those who have arisen from a swamp of deceit and lack true knowledge do not shine,
like *kiṃsuka* trees devoid of fragrance.
A low-born son who is a king’s minister,
a fool who is wise,
and much wealth for one who has no wealth.
Do not think highly of men who,
out of greed for their craft,
acquire that craft in great measure.
Like a mute seeing a dream,
I do not even dare to speak;
let the potter break [his pots].
He strikes the water-jar to make it shine,
not to cast it into the states of misery,
for the sake of the advancement of his disciples.
The man who wraps tagara with palāśa leaves— though it be but a leaf—
it wafts forth a fragrant scent.
Thus ends the section on associating with the wise.
The section on the fool is finished. Now begins the section on the good person (*sujana*).
One should associate only with the virtuous,
one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous;
having understood the true Dhamma of the noble ones, [one should dwell with them].
One becomes better, not worse.
Abandon association with the wicked and cultivate the company of the virtuous.
Perform meritorious deeds day and night;
constantly reflect upon impermanence,
just as one observes the ripening of the udumbara fruit.
And just as it is covered on the outside,
so too is the interior filled with worms— such is the heart of the wicked.
Just as when a jackfruit has ripened,
though it has thorns on the outside,
within it is endowed with ambrosia.
Thus are the hearts of the virtuous.
Even when dried, the sandalwood tree does not abandon its fragrance;
even when placed in the mouth of a man, the elephant does not abandon its grace.
The sugarcane, even when it has reached the press, does not give up its sweet juice;
likewise, even in the face of suffering, a wise person does not abandon the Dhamma.
Even when hungry, the lion—
He does not eat leaves and such;
though he is indeed emaciated,
the lion does not eat the flesh of elephants.
Born into a noble family, a son of good lineage,
well-guarded by his family’s tradition—
even though he has himself fallen into suffering—
One should not perform base actions.
Sandalwood is cool in this world,
but the moon is even cooler than that.
Better than the coolness of fierce sandalwood,
well-spoken words are excellent;
even the sun might rise in the west.
There was one named Merurāja;
there was coolness even in the heart of hell,
and a lotus grew upon the mountain peak.
It blossoms and never withers;
it is always worthy of praise.
Like the shade of a tree, it is pleasant.
Then for kinsmen, mother, and father;
then for the teacher and the king;
and then manifoldly for the Buddha.
Bees desire flowers;
the virtuous desire good qualities;
flies desire what is putrid.
The wicked desire two things:
harsh speech toward one who has failed his mother,
and misconduct toward one who has failed his father.
Both mother and father are inferior when they speak ill and act wickedly; but for a superior person,
it is the mother who speaks well.
The father of a merchant is well-performed;
both mother and father are excellent,
as are well-spoken words and good deeds.
In battle, they desire a hero;
among counselors, one who is free from curiosity;
and in food and drink, that which is dear.
But when a wise person is born,
a dog, upon seeing another dog,
shows its fangs in order to harm him.
When a wicked person sees a good person,
he seeks to harm them out of resentment.
Therefore, do not perform actions with impulsive haste.
Whether you do it yourself or cause it to be done,
the dull-witted person who acts with haste later regrets that deed.
Having abandoned anger, one never grieves;
the seers praised the abandonment of hypocrisy.
One should forgive the harsh words of everyone.
The virtuous call this patience supreme.
Dwelling in a cramped place, amidst impurity and fear, is suffering.
Therefore, one should advise and instruct even an enemy who is disliked,
and especially one who is ungrateful.
And one should restrain those who revile others;
for such a person is dear to the virtuous,
but is disliked by the wicked.
One should conquer the superior by means of patience,
the brave by means of stratagem,
and the inferior by means of small gifts.
One should conquer with effort as one's equal.
They say that poison is not truly poison;
it is said that the wealth of the Saṅgha is the real poison.
Poison kills but one person,
but everything belonging to the Saṅgha [kills] all;
they know the noble horse in its speed.
They know a bull by its carrying of the burden, a cow by its milking,
and a wise man by his speaking.
Even a small amount of wealth for the virtuous is a support, like water in a well;
but even a great deal for the wicked—
Nor does water drink water from the ocean;
rivers do not drink the water,
nor do trees eat the fruit.
In some places the clouds do not rain;
for the virtuous, wealth is for the sake of others.
One should not desire what is undesireable.
One should not think what is improper to think;
one should think only on the Dhamma,
so as not to let time pass in vain.
Even that which is not thought of comes to be,
and even that which is thought of perishes;
for wealth does not arise from mere thinking.
Whether it be a woman or a man,
one who is wicked is dear to those who are wicked,
but does not make himself dear to those who are virtuous.
One who delights in the teachings of the wicked—
this is a cause of ruin.
The Chapter on Good People is finished.
4. The Chapter on the Foolish Wicked Man:
One should not be overly affectionate toward a wicked man who creates a commotion.
Just as a jar filled half-full, even when carried on the head, [is dangerous],
so too is a wicked snake and a wicked person.
A wicked person is more venomous than a snake; that snake can be calmed by mantras and herbs,
but by what means is a wicked person appeased?
The fool who considers himself a fool is thereby wise;
but the fool who fancies himself wise is truly a fool.
Thus indeed is one called a fool:
the fool imagines himself to be like honey as long as his evil deed has not yet ripened.
And when the evil ripens,
then one encounters suffering.
It is not good for the fool to be powerful.
The one of poor wisdom quickly acquires wealth,
but with the breakup of the body,
he is reborn in hell.
A wicked rat in the house,
a wicked monkey in the forest,
and a wicked crow among birds—
A Brahmin who is corrupt among men;
long is the night for one who stays awake,
long is a league for one who is weary.
Long is the cycle of existence for fools who do not understand the True Dhamma,
even if they give as much as a single sesame seed to others.
The base-born person sees even a slight fault,
yet does not see the fault in a coconut, though it possesses one.
One should know the fault of another,
and one should know the fault in oneself;
like a tortoise with its limbs withdrawn into its shell, one should guard what is secret.
And one observes the faults of others.
While the wise are being praised,
punishment is meted out by the fool.
The wise man should be praised by the wise,
like gold that has been well-refined;
he should grasp what is beneficial with purpose.
One who is stubborn is won over by a gesture of respect;
one who is deluded by compliance with his whims is won over by flattery;
and a wise person is won over by the truth as it is.
The Chapter on the Foolish Wicked One is finished.
4. The Chapter on Friends:
A benefactor is a true kinsman; one who causes harm is no relative at all.
Even a kinsman is harmful if he is an outsider;
a disease born of one's own body is harmful,
while the forest medicine is beneficial.
One should avoid such a friend who destroys one's virtues behind one's back, even while speaking sweet words to one's face.
Just as one would discard honey from a poisoned jar,
so should one abandon a friend who lacks wealth—
even one's own children, wife, and siblings.
People serve one who possesses wealth;
in this world, wealth is a great friend.
One should know a servant by his conduct.
Likewise, one should support a kinsman when fear has come upon him, a friend in times of small means,
and a wife when wealth is exhausted.
He is a kinsman who is intent on one's welfare;
he is a father who provides support;
he is a friend in whom there is trust.
She is the wife of one who has attained peace.
One should not trust the untrustworthy,
nor should one trust even a friend.
Sometimes, when provoked,
a friend reveals all his faults;
yet one who has once been betrayed by a friend...
He desires to reconnect again;
he embraces death as a woman conceives a fetus.
One should carry an enemy on one's shoulder as long as the time has not yet come; but when that very time has arrived,
[one should strike him down].
Break the head like a jar.
[The words] *iṇaseso*, *aggiseso*,
and likewise *satruseso*;
They increase again and again;
therefore, one should not cause anything else to be done.
He whose face is like a lotus—
Speech may be cool as sandalwood,
yet one should not attend upon such a person if there is halāhala poison in their heart.
One should not serve a harsh master,
nor should one serve a miserly one; rather,
one should seek out a master who is free from such faults.
Not even a single nigrodha tree from that [forest] was taken;
for fifty siṅgī trees by the hand,
one should avoid a hundred horses.
One should give away an elephant that gives musth-ichor for a thousand coins,
but one should abandon a wicked person,
a bad country, and a bad friend.
One should avoid from afar a bad family, a bad friend, a bad wife, and a bad slave.
In times of illness and famine,
in calamity and conflict with enemies,
at the king’s gate and in the charnel ground—
Those who stand as true friends:
one who is cool in speech has many friends,
while the harsh one has few.
The similes here should be understood as those of the moon, the sun, and kings.
The section on friends is finished.
5. The section on women:
the cuckoo’s song as a form, the woman’s form, and devotion to a husband.
Knowledge is the beauty of those without form;
forbearance is the beauty of ascetics;
and for women, wealth is their beauty.
Knowledge is the wealth of men;
virtue is the wealth of bhikkhus;
and power is the wealth of kings.
The ascetic shines in his emaciation;
the quadruped shines in its bulk;
the man shines in his wisdom.
A woman is the mistress of beauty;
five are the delights of fragrance,
and seven are the delights of archery.
The wife is beautiful for one month;
the student is beautiful for half a month.
But the mud delights the pig.
The fool delights in what is harmful;
the woman delights in the man;
the man delights in the woman.
One should praise old food,
a wife whose youth has passed,
and a hero who has returned from battle.
And a house that has been entered by a snake;
a woman with two husbands,
and a bhikkhu who dwells as a companion to two [women].
Like a bird released from a double snare,
having employed many deceptions,
one should tame the wicked person with blows.
One who does not speak of taming is no friend; one who restrains a woman from calamity is a friend;
and for those with passion, moderation in eating is a friend.
The night is not without the moon,
nor is the ocean without its waves;
a lotus pond is not without the swan.
A maiden shines because of her husband.
Wealth produced by the husband is guarded by the woman alone.
For a man is like a spearhead,
a woman like a needle on a thread;
all rivers are crooked rivers.
All forests are made of wood;
all women commit evil when they find a secluded place.
One who is prone to quarreling, who speaks with envy,
who looks about with longing, who eats much and various kinds of food,
who eats as a guest, and who dwells in another's house—
A man should abandon even a hundred sons rather than a woman;
she is like a mistress when feasting on delicacies,
yet like a modest sister in private places.
When tasks arise, she acts like a servant;
in times of fear, she is a counselor; on the bed, she brings delight;
in matters of form, she is trained; and in difficult situations, she is patient.
The wise declare that she is the foremost of women;
with the breakup of the body, she shall be reborn in a heavenly realm.
She has eyes like a deer and a slender waist.
Fair-hipped, well-formed, with rows of even teeth,
deep-navelled, youthful, and virtuous— such a woman is to be wed,
even if born of a lowly family.
Of autumn and winter seasons, the rainy season is the best;
of wives, the beautiful one;
of sons, the eldest.
Of all directions, the northern direction is the best.
Whatever kind of person a man may wish to be,
birth after birth, again and again—
One should honor one's husband,
as female attendants honor Indra;
if a man wishes to be so, [he should act thus].
Birth after birth, again and again,
one should avoid giving to others,
just as one whose feet have been washed avoids mud.
When a man's youth has passed,
he brings home a Timbaru fruit; for her,
there is jealousy and lack of faith.
That is the cause of one's downfall.
The section on women is finished.
6. The Section on Kings.
The king sleeps for one watch,
the wise man for two watches,
and household life for three watches.
The one with four vows, the beggar, the wealthy man,
the learned man, the king, the river, and the physician— these are the five.
In whatever place these do not exist,
one should not dwell there for even a day;
in whatever region pride is not found.
There is no love, nor kinsmen;
there is no knowledge whatsoever gained there,
nor should one dwell there for even a single day.
A house is empty without a son;
a kingdom is empty without a king;
the mouth of a craft is empty without skill.
All is empty for the poor;
the merchant should desire wealth, and the student should desire knowledge and associate with the wise.
One who desires gain seeks out a young woman;
a king brings his minister under his control.
One who is dissatisfied is ruined.
The lord of the earth was contented,
the courtesan lost her sense of shame,
and the noble lady became utterly shameless.
The sky is the strength of birds,
water is the strength of fish;
for the weak, the king is their strength.
The crying of children is strength.
Patience, wakefulness, rising [from sleep], sharing, and compassion;
These are the qualities of a leader;
these are the qualities desired by the virtuous.
Kings speak of them but once.
Once in the world are recluses and brahmins, once are true persons;
this is the eternal law.
A lazy householder who indulges in sensual pleasures is not good;
a self-restrainedless renunciant is not good;
a king who acts without reflection is not good.
It is not good even for a wise man to be angry.
Where there are many leaders,
all of whom consider themselves wise;
All desire greatness, yet their karma perishes;
one should know for oneself both gain and loss.
The king himself [should oversee] what has been done and what remains to be done:
those who deserve restraint, he should restrain;
those worthy of support, he should support.
One should serve the husband with one's back like a pestle,
and with one's belly like the sacrificial fire;
[one should serve] the husband with every part of oneself.
One free from delusion [reaches] the next world.
Fire, water, women, snakes, and royal families— these are the five things that cause ruin for the foolish.
One must depart by fleeing;
those who carry away another's wife are swift-footed. Living with a corrupt wife—
One with a corrupted mind is a slave;
dwelling in a house with snakes,
death itself is certain— there is no doubt.
A deluded disciple [is led astray] by partiality,
by the support of a young wife,
and by association with the wicked.
The wise man desponds at the evil committed by his son, as he does at the evil committed by his pupil,
for he holds them dear.
The king conquers the evil of the realm, and the chaplain conquers the evil of the king.
One should conquer anger with non-anger.
Conquer the wicked with goodness;
conquer the miser with giving;
conquer the speaker of falsehood with truth.
Taming the untamed is generosity;
generosity is effective everywhere;
through generosity and pleasant speech, [one achieves success].
They rise and they fall;
generosity is the medicine for affection,
while stinginess is the antidote for hatred.
Generosity is the medicine for one of renown;
stinginess is the medicine for the wretched. Of many things that have little value, [generosity is the most significant].
One should conquer victory through harmony;
by means of grasses the rope is woven,
and by that even an elephant is bound.
Even if one's companion is incapable,
what can he do with his own splendor?
It is like a fire blazing in a windless place.
One attains peace for oneself.
One should never enjoy sensual pleasures as an equal to a king.
Gestures, tastes, or food,
garlands, scents, and ointments,
clothing, and all manner of ornaments—
Do not act as one equal to a king.
A king is not my friend,
nor is a king a partner for sexual intercourse.
"He is my husband"— thus one should firmly establish this conviction in the mind.
One should not associate with the king too closely.
One should not sit too close to another, nor on a seat that is straight, nor one that is too low;
one should not occupy a high seat.
A servant should avoid what is unwholesome and remain self-restrained like a fire;
even if equal in virtue and omniscience, [one should not neglect this].
Without support it does not shine;
even a priceless, supreme gem shines only by depending on gold.
The Chapter on Kings is finished.
7. The Miscellaneous Chapter: "In the case of one who is mixed with women, from where would there be virtue?"
How can there be compassion for one who eats meat?
How can there be truthfulness for one who drinks liquor?
How can there be moral shame in the presence of great greed?
O Mahātandi, from where comes skill?
O Mahākodha, from where comes wealth?
Wine, addiction, and untimely eating—where do they come from?
One who is lazy in practicing virtue,
a gambler addicted to sport, and one with evil friends—
these are the gateways to the destruction of wealth.
One should not look at her by day, nor speak with her at night;
one may move about with her only out of fear.
Like a forest-dweller in the woods,
even those who are living are described by Vyāsa as being as good as dead.
One who is suffering, diseased, deluded,
indebted, or a perpetual servant—
having seen the danger yet to come, [one should act].
One should avoid it from afar;
seeing danger approaching,
the wise person remains unafraid.
One who is drowsy and negligent, one who is intoxicated by pleasure, one who is afflicted by disease,
one who has great desire, and one who delights in worldly action—
Those beings are excluded from the caravan leader.
Go to misfortune, O gain!
For one who possesses gain is filled by gain.
When it rains on the dry land, O Pajjunna,
the Indus is filled by the rain;
this is not dependent solely on the power of karma.
For no one, when a task has been completed,
remains indifferent toward the doer;
therefore, all tasks [should be performed].
One should have it made with a small remnant.
Cotton is light in this world;
therefore, one who is prone to restlessness [should use it].
Then, heedless in the Buddha’s teaching,
he spoke words that were arrogant and heavy as a stone parasol.
Then the Devatānañcakkhaṇa;
then the Advice to the Elders;
then the Teaching of the Buddha.
The right hand is the body;
hatred is the little finger here;
the ears, nose, and eyes—
The left foot-rest is always guarded by Kuvera in the middle leaf of the betel-roll.
The yakṣa protects the root,
while the ill-omened one guards the tip;
one should eat those [fruits] after cutting them off.
In this way, prosperity increases:
one who guards all things well is like Brahmā,
while one who guards nothing at all is like a fish.
Therefore, indeed, let them honor him;
people always revere that man.
For he is like a bull among all householders.
They are providers and givers of wealth;
therefore, one should honor and revere them just like one's mother and father.
And those who eat beef,
they eat as if it were their mother’s flesh;
when those beings have died, vultures [will devour them].
One should cause [the work] to be carried out during the Dada and Sota periods. The commencement of a craft is successful when Jupiter is strong;
it is middling when the Sun and Venus are present.
On the first day [of the lunar fortnight], there is no craft;
on the second, the death of a son; on the third, the death of a wife;
on the eighth, it destroys the teacher.
One destroys one's craft on the fourteenth day; one destroys ten crafts on the full moon day,
as do one's mother and father.
One should not eat for seven days, nor for nine,
nor likewise for ten; one should not eat for twelve, nor for thirteen, nor for fourteen.
If one eats, one's craft perishes.
One should sacrifice an individual for the sake of a family; one should sacrifice a village for the sake of a nation.
One should abandon a village for the sake of a district;
one should abandon the earth for the sake of oneself.
Abandoning the country, they go forth.
The lion is a true man, as is the elephant;
they meet their end right there.
The crow is a base man, as is the deer.
In that place where there is no conceit,
no affection, and no relatives,
nor any grasping at knowledge—
One should not dwell there.
The wise person walks on one foot and stands on one foot.
Having reflected upon the higher state,
one should not abandon the former abode;
[this applies] to the employment of wealth and grain.
Likewise, regarding the acquisition of knowledge,
messengers, and services,
one should at that time abandon shamelessness and cultivate modesty.
Sloth and torpor have a twofold nutriment;
wisdom has a fourfold nutriment;
effort has a sixfold nutriment.
The kāma [scale] would have eight qualities.
In each successive stage, as it proceeds through the sequence of kamas,
it attains a superior essence and expression.
Likewise, one with good friends is virtuous;
the opposite person is wicked.
A farmer, a merchant, or a laborer—
The ascetic who is learned and virtuous—
if such as these are born in abundance,
the kingdom too will become abundant.
Lack of recitation is the stain of mantras;
lack of exertion is the stain of households;
laziness is the stain of beauty.
Heedlessness is the stain of the one who guards [his wealth]; it goes to the possession of the base,
while for the heroes it is their very essence.
The inferior people say that one's past karma is the primary factor;
the wise do not speak thus.
They exerted themselves in all their tasks;
if that task does not succeed,
what fault is there in its being fruitless?
A low-born family, or one lacking wisdom,
devoid of beauty and strength—
this is a time of ruin, a time of calamity.
Wealth alone is the distinguishing mark.
The Miscellaneous Chapter is finished.
The Chapter on the Wise Man and the Good Person.
The evil person, the wife of a friend,
the king, and miscellaneous topics—
thus it is adorned with seven sections.
By the Elder Visuddhācāra,
a dweller of the Visuddhārāma,
for the benefit of all families.
It has been purified at the destruction of the paths.
